idiom_name: deferred sequence value: element source/thunk + optional memo cell + lazy adapters + terminal forcing
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: expose a sequence-shaped value that produces element N+1 only when asked (pull: next()/iterator; push: a yield callback the consumer can stop), keep the producing state inside the sequence rather than in the consumer, and compose transformations as adapters that stay lazy - an adapter returns a new sequence and never a materialized collection. Decide and document the traversal contract explicitly: single-use or re-iterable, recomputing or memoizing; if elements are memoized, bound the retained prefix or provide a way to release it. Terminals (reduce, toList, for) are the only places that force elements, so validation, cleanup and resource release belong at the boundaries where forcing starts and stops.
code_sketch:
lazy(source):                        # nothing runs yet
    return DeferredSequence(source, adapters=[], cache=None)

seq = lazy(source).map(f).filter(p)  # adapters stay lazy
for x in seq.take(10):               # terminal: forces exactly what is asked
    consume(x)                       # early stop stops production
release(seq)                         # deterministic cleanup of the source
pitfalls: Memoizing without a bound retains the whole realized prefix (the classic lazy-list space leak); recomputing on every traversal duplicates expensive work instead.
Skipping the traversal contract turns a single-use iterator into a seemingly re-iterable collection: the second pass silently yields nothing.
Adapters that force elements (sort, count, group-by) destroy the laziness guarantee and hang on unbounded sources.
Closure captures (variable captures by reference in closures) can cause surprising retention of the entire surrounding scope long after the sequence is otherwise done.
Implicit resource holding: generators holding file handles, DB connections or goroutines survive past the expected end of iteration if not explicitly closed.

Wrong move: expose a lazy generator over a file after closing the file -> iteration fails mid-consumption or leaks lifetime assumptions -> instead keep the resource open for the forcing scope and close it deterministically.
Wrong move: call sort/count/toList on an unbounded sequence -> the terminal operation never completes and may exhaust memory -> instead bound it with take/limit or use a streaming aggregate.

Wrong move: promise re-iterable collection semantics for a single-use stream -> the second traversal throws or yields no elements -> instead document single-use and return a fresh sequence factory when repeat traversal is required.
